back: Whatever passes to the living at a person's death: property, rights, duties, a name, a position, knowledge.
The person chosen to succeed the deceased, taking over name, position and duties (Shona mugari wenhaka; Ndebele indlalifa).
Inheritance that can be seen and touched, e.g. cattle, tools, land-use rights.
Inheritance that cannot be touched, e.g. name, totem, language, values, a traditional office.
The sharing of a deceased person's estate (Shona), often at kurova guva.

front: Name three duties of an indigenous heir.
back: Caring for the widow; caring for and educating the children; keeping the family together and representing it.

front: Why was land not sold by an heir in indigenous society?
back: Land was not private property; families held use rights allocated through traditional leaders.

front: Give two weaknesses of indigenous inheritance.
back: Widows and daughters were often excluded from property; the system depended on the heir's honesty (also disputes, forced widow inheritance).

front: Give two strengths of indigenous inheritance.
back: Someone had a duty to care for widows and children; property and identity stayed within the family.
